442: Cluster analysis was then performed on all 30 cultivar and product combinations together, using the 22 attributes determined in every product. Ward's method resolved them into 3 groups, of which 2 contained a single product only (Table 59 and Fig. 51). When the products are compared with one another, therefore, it is the method of preparation rather than the cultivar that determines the broad quality type, whereas within any one product the cultivar is the variable under the processor's control. The two findings are complementary rather than contradictory: the preparation determines the type of product and the cultivar its standing within that type.
443: The cultivars identified here should be re-evaluated on a larger scale and over additional years before being recommended generally. For breeding work directed at improving the group as a whole, parents are best drawn from different clusters, since crosses between distant clusters are more likely to release useful variation.
447: Seven traditional products were prepared from nine aromatic rice cultivars of West Bengal together with Dudeshwar, a non-aromatic cultivar serving as the control. Four of the products are cooked, namely table rice, kichidi, pulao and payash, and three are processed, namely popped rice, puffed rice and flattened rice. Each was laid out in a completely randomised design with three replications and repeated over two years, the two years being analysed jointly as a pooled design. Between 22 and 25 quality attributes were determined in each product, covering the nutritional, bioactive, mineral, colour and sensory groups, yielding 162 attribute and product combinations in all.
449: The cultivar effect was significant in 157 of the 162 combinations, that is 96.9 per cent. The year effect was significant in 68 (42.0 per cent) and the year by cultivar interaction in 49 (30.2 per cent). The margin between these three figures constitutes the central result of the experiment: almost every attribute separated the cultivars, fewer than half separated the years, and fewer than a third exhibited any change in the magnitude of the cultivar differences between years. The identity of the cultivar therefore governs the quality of the finished product, the year of production exerts a smaller and less consistent effect, and the ranking of the cultivars is largely stable from one year to the next. In practical terms, a cultivar chosen on one year of data may be expected to retain its position in the following year.
450: Coefficients of variation were low throughout, which demonstrates that the trials were well controlled and that the differences reported are not an artefact of experimental error. Table B sets out the position for each product separately.
454: Since the analysis of variance addresses one attribute at a time, and since a high value is favourable for certain attributes and a low value for others, a single figure was required to rank the cultivars overall. This was obtained by the total quality scoring approach of Ismail et al. (2001), whose validity as a measure of overall quality was subsequently examined by Kraggerud et al. (2012). Every attribute on which the cultivars differed significantly was scored from 0 to 100 in the favourable direction, averaged within the five groups, and combined by weight, sensory carrying 30 per cent, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10.
455: On this index the superior cultivar was Gobindabhog for payash and popped rice, Kalojira for table rice, Radhunipagal for kichidi, Kataribhog for pulao, Radhatilak for puffed rice and Harinakhuri for flattened rice. No single cultivar proved superior for all seven products, so that the choice of raw material must follow the product intended. Kalojira appeared among the first three in four products, and Gobindabhog, Kalonunia and Radhatilak in three each, so that these four are the entries of widest utility across the group.
456: The control ranked last of the ten entries in six of the seven products and ninth in the seventh. The margin between the superior cultivar and the control ranged from 16.5 points in puffed rice to 45.7 in payash. Substituting the cultivars named here for Dudeshwar would therefore raise the quality of every product appreciably, and would do so without any alteration in the method of preparation.
457: How far the ranking can be relied upon
458: The weights employed in the index were assigned rather than computed, and the ranking was therefore verified against a second set of weights derived from the data. Principal component analysis was applied to the merit scores, and each attribute was weighted by the sum, over the components with an eigenvalue of one or more, of its squared loading multiplied by the share of variance that component carries. Taking the seven products together, the mean rank correlation between the two rankings was 0.946, the minimum 0.867, and the same cultivar ranked first in 6 of the seven. The ranking is therefore a property of the data and not of the weights adopted. Where the two diverged, the cultivars concerned were in any case closely positioned on the index.
459: A second and entirely independent check is afforded by the count of attributes on which each cultivar exceeded the control, which employs no weights at all. The cultivar with the best net balance coincided with the cultivar of highest index in three of the seven products, and in the remainder the two entries were again closely positioned on the index. Taken together, the two checks demonstrate that the recommendations do not depend upon the particular scheme by which the index was constructed.
460: Principal component analysis is employed here solely to assign the weights. The components themselves cannot rank the cultivars for quality, since a component measures the direction of greatest variation and takes no account of whether a high or a low value is the more desirable.
462: Cluster analysis was performed on all 70 cultivar and product combinations across the two parts, using the attributes determined in every product of each part. Ward's method yielded 7 groups, of which 5 contained a single product only. The clusters therefore correspond to products rather than to cultivars. When one preparation is compared with another it is the method of preparation, not the cultivar, that determines the broad quality type; within any one preparation the cultivar is the variable under the processor's control. The two findings are complementary rather than contradictory: the preparation fixes the type of product and the cultivar fixes its standing within that type.
464: The quality of these seven traditional products is determined principally by the cultivar from which they are prepared. Nine of the ten entries evaluated proved superior to the non-aromatic control, and for each product a specific cultivar may be recommended: Gobindabhog for payash and popped rice, Kalojira for table rice, Radhunipagal for kichidi, Kataribhog for pulao, Radhatilak for puffed rice and Harinakhuri for flattened rice. These recommendations rest upon a composite quality score index shown to be insensitive to the weights employed and to accord with an unweighted count against the control. Where a processor prepares more than one of these products, Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Kalonunia and Radhatilak are the entries performing well across the widest range.
465: Three qualifications should be stated. First, the index ranks these ten entries relative to one another and does not constitute an absolute scale, so that it would require recomputation were further cultivars added. Second, the trials covered two years at one location, and confirmation over additional years and sites is required before any general recommendation is issued. Third, the weights placed upon the five attribute groups reflect a judgement as to their relative importance, and a processor whose market rests chiefly upon one aspect of quality would be justified in recomputing the index under weights of their own.
466: For breeding work directed at improving this group of cultivars, parents are best drawn from different clusters, since crosses between distant clusters are the more likely to release useful variation. The cultivars identified here also merit evaluation in products beyond the seven examined, since the cluster analysis indicates that each preparation makes its own demands of the raw material.
